objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a level turn works at shallow, medium and steep bank, demonstrate a coordinated level turn and a rollout on a named heading while explaining it from the right seat, and spot, explain and fix the errors learners make in their first turns.
why: Turns are one of the four fundamentals, and every later maneuver is built from them; gaps here become barriers later [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. The level turn is also where a learner first meets adverse yaw, back pressure and the sight picture of a banked horizon [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. As the instructor you have to fly it cleanly while talking, then read a learner's turn and name the cause of each error.

prereading.label: AFH 3-11 to 3-17
prereading.what: Level turns: what each control does, shallow/medium/steep classes, adverse yaw, slip and skid, cowling and posture references, parallax, rudder timing cues, rollout lead and the 11 common errors. The core reading.

prereading.label: AFH 3-1 to 3-10
prereading.what: The four fundamentals, light grip and feel, attitude flying, integrated flight instruction (90/10) and trim technique.

prereading.label: PHAK 5-22 to 5-23
prereading.what: Forces in turns: horizontal and vertical lift, why the rudder does not turn the airplane, power in turns, slipping and skidding turns.

prereading.label: PHAK 6-3 to 6-4, 8-17 to 8-18
prereading.what: Adverse yaw and the control inputs for a coordinated turn; the turn coordinator, inclinometer and "step on the ball."

prereading.label: AIH 9-7 to 9-12
prereading.what: The AIH sample level turn demonstration, use of distractions, integrated flight instruction, see and avoid, and correcting learner errors.

prereading.label: AIH 3-30 to 3-31
prereading.what: Task management, fixation and inattention, and how to spot fixation by watching the learner's eyes.

prereading.label: AIM 4-4-15

warmup: Think first: your learner rolls into a 30° left turn. The nose swings right for a moment, then the altimeter slowly unwinds, and on the rollout the airplane sails 15° past the heading you asked for. That is three separate errors. What caused each one, which would you fix first, and what would you say in the air so the next turn is better?

key_terms.def: The part of total lift that acts toward the center of the turn once the wings are banked; it is what turns the airplane, not the rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].
The part of total lift that opposes weight in a bank. It shrinks as bank increases, so the pilot raises the angle of attack to keep it equal to weight and hold altitude [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
About 20° or less, about 20° to 45°, and about 45° or more. Shallow banks tend to level, medium banks hold, steep banks keep rolling in [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
The yaw away from the turn caused by the extra drag of the wing whose aileron goes down to raise it; most pronounced at low airspeed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].

A turn with rudder applied together with aileron to cancel adverse yaw, so the nose and tail track the same path and the ball stays centered [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]] [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
The rate of turn is too slow for the bank; the ball moves to the inside of the turn and the pilot feels pushed toward the inside [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
The rate of turn is too great for the bank; the ball moves to the outside of the turn and the pilot feels pushed toward the outside [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
The ball in a curved, fluid-filled tube that shows yaw. Center it with rudder on the side the ball is deflected: "step on the ball" [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Starting the rollout before the desired heading because the airplane keeps turning while banked; the rule of thumb is half the bank angle [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Teaching each maneuver by outside references and flight instruments together, starting the first time the maneuver is introduced [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Unintended pressure on one control axis while moving another, such as adding pitch when only bank was intended [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
A turn made to be certain the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's flightpath; teach it and insist on it before all turns [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the CFI standard

body.p: The four fundamentals are straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs and descents. All flying tasks are built from them, and moving on to advanced maneuvers before they are mastered hinders learning. The instructor's job is to give the learner enough command of them to combine them at least at ACS level [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. A takeoff, a departure and an approach are all built from these pieces [[24:62|AFH 3-1]].

The AFH gives the level turn as a short sequence: bank the airplane, adding enough power or pitching up to make up for the lost vertical lift; neutralize the controls as needed to stop the bank from increasing and hold the bank; use opposite aileron to return to level; and neutralize the ailerons, with a power or pitch reduction, for level flight [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].

bullets: Ailerons bank the wings and set the rate of turn for a given airspeed [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].
Elevator pitches the nose relative to the pilot; without added power the pilot raises the pitch slightly to replace the lift used for turning [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].
Throttle gives thrust for airspeed control and can vary the radius of the turn [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].
Rudder offsets adverse yaw from the wings and the engine and propeller. The rudder does not turn the airplane [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].

body.p: The CFI ACS gives no altitude, bank or heading tolerance for this Task. Application: hold yourself to the standard your learners will need, a steady altitude, a steady bank, a centered ball and a rollout on the heading you named, and say each number out loud as you fly.

callout.text: Load factor and stall speed in turns are taught in AI.II.D (Principles of Flight), and overbanking at 45° and beyond in AI.IX.A (Steep Turns). This lesson stays with the everyday level turn and how to teach it.

check.q: What do the two CFI skill elements for this Task ask, and what numeric tolerance does the ACS give?
check.a: Establish, maintain and roll out of a level turn while simultaneously explaining it, and analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VIII.B.S1, S2). The CFI ACS lists no numeric tolerance for this Task.

body.p: In a bank, total lift tilts with the wings and splits into a vertical component that opposes weight and a horizontal component that pulls the airplane toward the center of the turn. It is the horizontal component that turns the airplane, not the rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The PHAK calls it centripetal force, with centrifugal force as the equal and opposite reaction [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

bullets: An airplane is not steered like a boat or a car. It must be banked to turn, and once banked it turns unless it is slipping to the inside [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

Banking alone does not change total lift. The vertical part gets smaller, so the airplane loses altitude unless the angle of attack is raised until vertical lift again equals weight [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

The extra angle of attack adds induced drag, so airspeed drops in proportion to the bank: a little in a shallow bank, a lot in a steep one. The added power needed is also proportional to the bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
At a given airspeed the rate of turn depends on the horizontal component, which grows with bank, so bank is how you control the rate of turn [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
The vertical fin makes no lift in straight flight; its job is to keep the tail behind the nose [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].

body.p: Rate of turn in degrees per second is 1,091 times the tangent of the bank, divided by true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. Application: at 100 knots and 20° of bank that is 1,091 x 0.364 / 100 = about 4° per second.

callout.text: Aileron to bank, bank to turn, back pressure to stay level, power to keep the speed, rudder to keep it clean.

check.q: A learner says she presses the left rudder pedal "to make the airplane turn left." How do you correct the idea?
check.a: The horizontal component of lift turns the airplane once it is banked; the rudder only offsets adverse yaw so the turn is coordinated [[24:72|AFH 3-11]] [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

chunks.title: Shallow, medium and steep: what the airplane does after roll-in

body.p: The AFH sorts turns by how the airplane behaves once the bank is set, and each class needs a different hand on the aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

Lateral stability slowly levels the wings [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]

body.p: In every class, back pressure stays in: the vertical component of lift has to be kept if altitude is to be kept. Airspeed loss is generally not significant in shallow banks; in steeper turns more power may be needed [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

bullets: Beginners should use small aileron and rudder inputs. Large inputs give fast roll rates and little time to evaluate and correct; smaller inputs give slower rolls and time to get pitch and bank right [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

The ailerons set both roll rate and bank. The rate depends on how much aileron is used; the bank depends on how long it is held, since the airplane keeps rolling as long as the ailerons are deflected [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

callout.text: Application: in the air, let the learner feel the classes with a light grip. Set 15°, relax the aileron and watch the wings creep back toward level; set 30°, relax, and watch the bank stay put. The learner then knows why "neutral" works in one turn and not the other.

check.q: A learner rolls into a 15° bank, neutralizes the aileron and a minute later is almost wings level and well short of the heading. Why?
check.a: In a shallow bank the airplane's inherent lateral stability slowly levels the wings unless aileron pressure is held into the bank [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

body.p: When the pilot rolls right, the left aileron goes down, raising the left wing with more lift and more drag. That drag yaws the nose toward the rising wing, opposite the direction of the bank: adverse yaw [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]. It is more pronounced at low airspeed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]], and the rudder needed to cancel it is greatest at low airspeed, high angle of attack and large aileron deflection [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. Differential and Frise-type ailerons reduce adverse yaw but do not eliminate it [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].
The fix is rudder pressure in the direction of the turn, applied at the same time as the aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The nose tells you about the timing [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]:

bullets: Nose starts to move before the bank starts: rudder applied too soon [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Bank starts before the nose turns, or the nose moves the opposite way: rudder applied too late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Nose moves up or down on entry: too much or too little elevator back pressure [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Slip: rate of turn too slow for the bank, ball to the inside of the turn. Correct with less bank, more rate of turn, or both [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Skid: rate of turn too great for the bank, ball to the outside. Correct with more bank, less rate of turn, or both [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Either way, "step on the ball": press the rudder on the side the ball is deflected [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Feel it too: the pilot is pressed toward the outside in a skid and toward the inside in a slip. A pilot should become sensitive to this without undue reliance on the instruments [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
A yaw string trails straight back when the airplane is coordinated [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

callout.text: Holding uncoordinated control deflections can set up a spin, and that is especially hazardous at low altitude such as the traffic pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. Coordination habits learned in level turns are the ones the learner will carry to the base-to-final turn.

check.q: In a right turn the ball sits left of center and the learner feels pushed to the left. What is it, and what is the rudder fix?
check.a: A skid: the ball is to the outside of the turn [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Step on the ball, which here means easing off the right rudder (left rudder pressure), or add bank or slow the rate of turn [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

chunks.title: Back pressure, power and trim in the turn

body.p: Hold the yoke or stick lightly with the fingers. A closed-palm grip kills the sensitive feel a learner needs, and the AFH suggests dealing with that habit at the start of training. It is control pressure, not control surface movement, that gets the result [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

bullets: Elevator: a turn needs more lift than straight flight, so back pressure goes in as the bank goes in, and the steeper the turn the more back pressure [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. Hold it constant to keep altitude [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

Power: the AFH sequence says to add enough power or pitch up to make up for the lost vertical lift [[24:72|AFH 3-11]]; airspeed loss is small in shallow banks and steeper turns may need more power [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. The AIH sample demonstration adds power slightly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Trim: the AIH demonstration says to neutralize the ailerons at the desired bank and trim as appropriate, then reduce power and trim on reaching wings level [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The AFH adds that trimming extra back pressure past about 30° may help, depending on the purpose of the turn and the force needed [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

Trim relieves pressure after the attitude is set; set the attitude first, then trim. Trying to fly the airplane with the trim is a common fault even among experienced pilots [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

body.p: Cross-coupling: elevator and aileron share one control, so beginners often add pitch when they meant only to bank. With a stick held in the right hand, diving in right turns and climbing in left turns is common because the arm pivots at the elbow. A control wheel may be less prone to this. The cure is practice and keeping the sight picture of the nose following the horizon [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

callout.text: Application of AFH 3-16 and AIH 9-7: if your learner trims in the turn, make "back pressure out, trim forward" part of every rollout callout, or the nose will rise as the wings come level.

check.q: Your learner trimmed nose-up in a long 30° turn. On rollout the nose comes up and the airplane climbs. What is going on and what is the fix?
check.a: The trim is still holding back pressure. Forward elevator pressure may be needed until the trim is readjusted [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

chunks.title: Visual references and the sight picture

body.p: Attitude is the angle between an airplane axis and the natural horizon. In VMC the pilot judges it from the wings and cowling against the horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]]. For bank, the fairly flat top of the cowling against the horizon is a reasonable first reference; then cross-check the attitude indicator to confirm the bank [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

Posture matters. A common problem is leaning away from the turn to stay upright relative to the horizon, and the AFH says to correct it immediately if the pilot is to learn the visual references [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

bullets: Pitch: keep a reference point on the nose fixed against the natural horizon, as in level flight, and cross-check the instruments [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. If altitude is drifting in the turn, correct the pitch against the horizon, then cross-check [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Keep the nose following the horizon and isolate any unwanted motion [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Bank: the wingtips are the primary reference for level bank in straight flight [[24:69|AFH 3-8]], and holding bank by watching only the nose is a listed level turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

Parallax: from the left seat the nose seems to rise in a left turn and descend in a right turn, because the pilot sits left of the roll axis [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. No source here covers the right seat; AI.IX.A gives an application for it.
Teaching aid: a dry erase marker or removable tape can mark reference lines on the windshield or cowling for a short while, until the learner knows where to look [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

callout.text: Application: before the flight, sit with the learner in the airplane and point out the cowling line, the nose reference and both wingtips. Then tell them what each will do in a left and a right turn, so the first turn in the air has no surprises.

check.q: From the left seat, why might a learner gain altitude in right turns while trying to hold the same sight picture used in left turns?
check.a: AFH 3-15: from the left seat the nose seems to descend in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: a learner who holds the level-flight picture raises the nose and climbs. Teach a separate picture for each direction and cross-check the altimeter [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

body.p: The airplane keeps turning as long as it is banked, so the rollout has to start before the desired heading. The lead depends on the bank; the rule of thumb is half the bank angle, so at 30° lead by 15° [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

bullets: The rollout is the roll-in with the controls reversed: aileron and rudder toward the high wing [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Relax elevator pressure as the bank decreases, as needed to hold altitude, and relax all pressures smoothly so the controls are neutral as the wings come level [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
If trim was used, forward pressure may be needed until the trim is adjusted [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Watch the outside references and the instruments to confirm the wings are level and the turn has stopped [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Half the bank is a good starting rule; the lead really depends on the type of turn, the turn rate and the rollout rate, and pilots develop a consistent technique with experience [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

callout.text: Application: the most common rollout errors combine. A learner who leads too little and also leaves the back pressure in finishes past the heading and climbing. Name one error at a time.

check.q: A learner keeps overshooting by about 10° when rolling out of 30° turns. What do you coach?
check.a: Start the rollout earlier, about 15° (half the bank) before the heading [[24:77|AFH 3-16]], and look at the roll-out rate, since the lead also depends on it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

body.p: Integrated (composite) instruction uses outside references and flight instruments together to set and hold attitude and performance [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]. The AIH says the instrument references should start the first time each maneuver is introduced, with no difference in how the controls are used whichever reference is in use [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. It begins with the first briefing on the flight controls, which covers both the instrument indications and the outside references [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

bullets: About 90 percent of attention outside on the horizon and traffic; no more than about 10 percent inside, in quick checks [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Control attitude by the horizon, confirm with the instruments, and make any correction against the horizon [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

A bank error obvious at the wingtips may be imperceptible on the attitude indicator to a beginner, and a pitch change of several inches on the horizon is a tiny move of the reference bar [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
The most common beginner error is correcting pitch or bank while still looking inside; beginners also fixate on instruments and "chase" them because of lag and precession [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
For the first several hours an instructor may cover the flight instruments to build outside skills or break a fixation habit [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

head: In a level turn, look at
It tells you
rows: Attitude indicator
Bank angle of the wings against the horizon [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]
Turn coordinator
Rate and direction of turn, not bank; the second mark is standard rate, 3° per second [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]
Ball (inclinometer)
Coordination; step on the ball [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]
Altimeter
Whether the pitch is holding altitude; if not, fix the pitch on the horizon and recheck [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Heading indicator
How far to the rollout heading [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]

callout.text: Make sure the learner understands that this does not prepare them for IMC. VFR flight into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatalities [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

check.q: Your learner flies a neat 30° turn but never looks outside. What does the AFH offer to break the habit?
check.a: Cover the flight instruments for a while to force outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]], and aim for about 90 percent of attention outside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

body.p: Teach level turns right after straight-and-level (AI.VIII.A) and before climbs and descents (AI.VIII.C and D): the fundamentals are built one on another, and deficiencies in them become barriers later [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. When a skill builds on one already learned, the known-to-unknown approach works; when several skills are taught at once, go simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
The AIH uses the level turn as its sample demonstration. Its talk-through, step by step [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]:

head: AIH sample demonstration step
Why it is in the script
rows: Use outside visual references and monitor the flight instruments
Integrated instruction from the first time the maneuver is shown [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
After clearing, add a little power, bank, add slight back pressure, rudder in the direction of the turn
Clearing before every turn [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]; back pressure for vertical lift [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]
Ailerons set roll rate and bank; neutralize at the desired bank, trim as appropriate
The airplane rolls as long as the ailerons are deflected [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Lead the rollout by about half the bank, coordinated aileron and rudder, release back pressure
All pressures neutral as the wings come level [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
At wings level, reduce power and trim
Back to the straight-and-level picture [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]

bullets: Teach both directions in the same lesson: gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction is a listed error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]], and the sight picture differs left and right [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].
Start the learner with small inputs and slow roll rates [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

Teach feel on purpose: in a banked turn the pilot is pressed down into the seat, and the instructor should teach the difference between perceiving these cues and merely noticing them [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: a slow altitude drift in a 20° turn is a safe one to let run for a few seconds.

If a learner flies it right but may not understand it, have them vary it slightly or combine it with another operation [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: ask for a 20° turn to a named heading, then a 40° turn back, and listen to what changes.

callout.text: Application: practice the AIH talk-through on the ground until you can say it while flying without losing altitude. On the CFI test you demonstrate and simultaneously explain (ACS AI.VIII.B Skills), and talking is what usually costs the altitude.

check.q: Why teach left and right level turns in the same lesson instead of mastering one direction first?
check.a: Proficiency in only one direction is a listed level turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]], and parallax makes the sight picture different in each direction [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

body.p: Most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying, and the real danger was inadvertent stalls from distractions in routine flight. The most effective training creates distractions while the learner practices maneuvers [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. AIH examples that suit turns include working out a heading to an airport from a chart, identifying a field for a forced landing and reversing course after S-turns [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

bullets: Task prioritization: before stacking tasks, make sure each can be done reasonably well on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

Fixation, absorption in one task while others slip, often means too little practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Spot it by glancing at the learner's eyes; a gaze stuck on one instrument is the sign [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Situational awareness includes aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft and the environment; budgeting time and prioritizing tasks give room to work without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Loss of situational awareness or disorientation: the body cannot tell gravity from the forces of maneuvering; in VMC the eyes usually win [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

The leans: a gradual, prolonged turn below about 2° per second goes unnoticed, and leveling the wings then feels like a bank the other way, so the pilot may lean into the original turn [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Coriolis illusion: a head movement in a different plane during a prolonged turn can create a false sense of rotation; retrieve dropped items with minimal head movement [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Seat-of-the-pants sensations give false cues in uncoordinated turns and turbulence [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

With no visible horizon, such as haze over the ocean, it is IMC for practical purposes [[24:65|AFH 3-4]], and relying on body sense alone leads to disorientation and loss of control [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

callout.text: Application: in a turn, pick distractions that keep the learner's head up and eyes outside, like finding a forced landing field, and save the dropped pencil for straight flight (see the Coriolis note above).

check.q: After a long, gentle left turn, your learner levels the wings and leans to the left, saying the airplane feels banked right. What is happening?
check.a: The leans: the slow turn went unnoticed by the inner ear, and leveling the wings creates a sense of banking the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Have the learner trust the horizon and attitude indicator.

body.p: A clearing procedure makes sure the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's path. Teach one from the start, insist on it, and have the learner use it before all turns and training maneuvers; with good scanning it is the most effective defense against collision [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Before a turn in a high-wing airplane, momentarily raise the wing in the direction of the turn and look; in a low-wing airplane, momentarily lower it and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]] [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].
The airplane's attitude creates its own blind spots [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]]; move your head to see around door posts and wings, and lift a wing when needed [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Have the learner call out "clear left, right, above, and below" [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].
Scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, each area held at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
A target with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Haze and smoke cut detection, and traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Practice areas can be crowded, and haze makes the hazard worse; tell the learner that you both share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. If learners think the instructor does all the scanning they never build the habit, and any tendency to start a maneuver without checking for traffic must be corrected at once. In one study, flight instructors were aboard in 37 percent of midair collisions [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Failure to adequately clear in the direction of the turn is the first error on the AFH level turn list [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Application: make the wing raise or dip and the spoken "clear right" the first move of every turn you demonstrate.

check.q: In a low-wing trainer, what does the AIM say to do just before a right turn?
check.a: Momentarily lower the right wing and look for traffic before turning [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

body.p: The AFH lists 11 common level turn errors [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. For S2 the examiner will fly some of them; name what you see, explain the cause, and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not clearing in the direction of the turn
Rolls in without a look or a wing raise
Clear before every turn and correct it at once [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Gaining or losing altitude
Nose drifts against the horizon; altimeter moving
Keep the back pressure in; fix pitch on the horizon, then cross-check [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Not holding the bank constant
Shallow bank decays, or bank creeps
Aileron into a shallow bank, neutral in a medium one [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Turning solely by instruments
Eyes inside the whole turn
About 90 percent outside; cover the instruments for a while [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Leaning away from the turn
Head and body tilted toward the high wing
Correct posture at once [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]
No feel for slips or skids
Ball off center and the learner does not notice
Teach the seat push of a slip or skid before looking at the ball [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]
Holding bank by the nose alone
Bank wanders while the nose looks fine
Cowling line and wingtips, then the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Skidding flat turns to avoid banking
Rudder yaws the nose, little bank, ball outside
The airplane turns by banking [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]; coordinate aileron and rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]
Excessive rudder in the direction of turn
Ball to the outside of the turn
Step on the ball: ease the inside rudder [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]
Proficiency in only one direction
Good left turns, poor right ones
Practice both; teach each sight picture [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]
Failure to coordinate the controls
Nose moves before or after the bank
Rudder with aileron; use the nose timing cues [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]

body.p: Two more show up on entry and rollout. If the nose moves up or down as the bank goes in, the back pressure is too much or too little [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Correcting pitch or bank while still looking inside is the most common beginner error of all [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

How to analyze: when the learner flies and talks, you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. If a deficiency needs reteaching, demonstrate it again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Application: fix the cause, not the number. "You lost 100 feet" helps less than "your back pressure came out when you looked at the heading indicator."

check.q: On the rollout from a left turn, the left wing comes up but the nose keeps swinging left for a moment. What is the timing error?
check.a: Rudder is late on the rollout. The rollout is the roll-in reversed, aileron and rudder together toward the high wing [[24:77|AFH 3-16]], and the bank moving before the nose follows means rudder too late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

f1.alt: A pilot's view in a left bank: the horizon tilts across the windshield above a town and an airport, an inset shows the lowered left wing against the ground, and below are round gauges and a glass display whose attitude indicators show a left bank.

f2.caption: Figure 3-11. When the airplane is banked into a turn, total lift is the resultant of two components: vertical and horizontal. (AFH 3-12)
f2.alt: Two head-on views. Left: level flight with lift straight up and weight straight down. Right: a steeply banked turn; total lift tilts with the wings and splits into a vertical component and a horizontal component; centrifugal force and weight combine into a larger resultant load.

f3.caption: Figure 3-12. The rudder opposes adverse yaw to help coordinate the turn. (AFH 3-13)
f3.alt: A light airplane rolling into a left turn over a town. The rising right wing has a large More lift arrow and additional induced drag; the lowered left wing has a Reduced lift arrow. A red arrow at the nose shows adverse yaw, and a box says the rudder opposes adverse yaw to coordinate the turn.

f4.caption: Figure 8-22. If inadequate right rudder is applied in a right turn, a slip results. Too much right rudder causes the aircraft to skid through the turn. Centering the ball results in a coordinated turn. (PHAK 8-18)
f4.alt: Three turn coordinators, each with the miniature airplane banked right. Slipping turn: the ball sits right of center, inside the turn. Skidding turn: the ball sits left of center, outside the turn. Coordinated turn: the ball is centered.

f5.alt: Two cockpit views in a bank, one with round gauges and one with a glass display. In each, a red line runs along the top of the instrument panel and cowling, tilted against the distant horizon, and a curved arrow marks the reference angle between them.

f6.alt: Two front views of a banked high-wing airplane. Left, labeled correct posture: a green pilot figure sits upright in line with the cabin. Right, labeled incorrect posture: a red figure leans away from the turn to stay upright with the horizon.

f7.alt: A view from a high-wing airplane cockpit with a glass display and round gauges, and a pie chart: a large green 90 percent slice and a small red 10 percent slice. A banner says 90 percent of the pilot's attention should be outside the flight deck and no more than 10 percent inside.

scenario.title: Third lesson: level turns with a pre-solo learner
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your learner, in the left seat of a high-wing trainer, flies solid straight-and-level and today starts level turns at shallow and medium bank, both directions. The day is hazy and the practice area sits near a VOR with other trainers in it. On the first turns you see four things: the learner leans away from each turn, the eyes stay on the attitude indicator, altitude drops in left turns and climbs in right turns, and the ball swings out during rollouts.

questions.q: Which outside and instrument references do you point out on the ground before the learner's first turn?
questions.a: Both outside and instrument references from the first introduction, with the controls used the same way for either [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; about 90 percent of attention outside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]; and the cowling, nose and wingtip references for each direction [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

questions.q: How do you handle clearing on this hazy day near the VOR?
questions.a: Before each turn the learner raises the wing toward the turn, looks, and calls the clearing [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Haze cuts detection and traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]; you both share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: Why fix the leaning right away instead of later?
questions.a: Leaning away from the turn spoils the visual references the learner is trying to learn, and the AFH says to correct it immediately [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

questions.q: Altitude drops in left turns and rises in right turns. What is the likely cause and the fix?
questions.a: Parallax: from the left seat the nose seems to rise in left turns and descend in right turns [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: the learner chases that false picture, lowering the nose in left turns and raising it in right ones. Teach a separate picture for each direction and cross-check the altimeter [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

questions.q: What does the stare at the attitude indicator tell you, and what do you do?
questions.a: Fixation, which you can spot by watching the eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; correcting while looking inside is the most common beginner error. Cover the instruments for a while to force outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

questions.q: The ball swings out during rollouts. What do you say?
questions.a: Roll out with aileron and rudder together toward the high wing, and relax the back pressure as the bank comes out [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Have the learner feel for the sideways push in the seat, not only watch the ball [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

skills.do: Establish, maintain, and roll out of a level turn while simultaneously explaining it (ACS AI.VIII.B.S1): clear in the direction of the turn, roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder, set back pressure and power, hold the bank and altitude, and roll out on a heading you named. The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance here, so the examiner judges whether altitude, bank and coordination are held and whether your explanation matches what you fly.
skills.practice: Fly left and right pairs at 20° and 30° while saying the AIH talk-through out loud [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; call the rollout lead before you start it [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]; have a second pilot tell you whenever your words and your hands disagree.

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.VIII.B.S2): watch the examiner fly a flawed turn, name each error from the AFH list, explain the cause, and give a specific fix, taking the controls if needed.
skills.practice: Have a fellow applicant fly each of the 11 AFH errors on purpose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] plus the rudder-timing and pitch-on-entry cues [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]; diagnose aloud within one turn and coach the fix in one short sentence.

quiz.q: In a coordinated level turn, which force pulls the airplane off its straight path?
options: The horizontal component of lift acting toward the center
The rudder's side force yawing the nose toward the center
Centrifugal force pushing the airplane around the curved flight path
The vertical component of lift tilted by the ailerons
quiz.why: The horizontal component of lift turns the airplane; the rudder only coordinates [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

quiz.q: Once a learner has set 30° of bank, what should the aileron be doing in most trainers?
options: Moving in small rhythmic inputs to hold the bank
Holding light opposite pressure to stop overbanking
Holding light pressure into the turn to keep the bank
Neutralized, because a medium bank tends to stay put on its own
quiz.why: At medium banks (about 20° to 45°) the bank tends to stay constant, so aileron and rudder are neutralized [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

quiz.q: When is the most rudder needed to cancel adverse yaw?
options: Low airspeed only when flaps are retracted fully
Low airspeed, high angle of attack, large aileron inputs
High airspeed with large aileron inputs at cruise power
High airspeed, low angle of attack and small aileron deflections
quiz.why: Rudder needed is greatest at low airspeeds, high angles of attack and large aileron deflections [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].

quiz.q: A learner is in a 20° bank. By the AFH rule of thumb, how far before the heading should the rollout begin?
In a skidding turn, where is the ball and what is wrong?
options: Inside the turn; the rate of turn is too slow for the bank angle
Centered; bank too steep for the airspeed
Outside the turn; rate of turn too great for the bank
Inside the turn; too much rudder into the turn
quiz.why: In a skid the rate of turn is too great for the bank and the ball moves to the outside [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

quiz.q: What should the elevator back pressure do while the bank is held in a level turn?
options: Be replaced with added power alone
Be held to keep the vertical lift
Be traded for more rudder pressure
Be released once the bank is set
quiz.why: Back pressure should not be relaxed; the vertical component of lift must be kept to keep altitude [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

quiz.q: In integrated flight instruction, about how much of the learner's attention should be inside the flight deck?
options: No more than about 10 percent
About 25 percent, in long looks
About half, more in turns than straight
About 90 percent, with quick glances outside
quiz.why: About 90 percent outside and no more than about 10 percent inside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Which reference does the AFH give for first setting the bank angle?
options: The heading indicator's rate of change
The turn coordinator's standard-rate mark for the bank you want
The top of the cowling against the natural horizon
The position of the ball in the inclinometer
quiz.why: The fairly flat top of the cowling against the horizon is a reasonable first bank reference; then cross-check the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, what should the pilot of a high-wing airplane do just before turning?
options: Lower the wing on the side opposite the turn and look
Raise the wing in the direction of the turn and look for traffic
Make two 90° turns in opposite directions first
Turn on the landing light and climb 200 feet
quiz.why: High-wing: momentarily raise the wing in the direction of the intended turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

options: A skidding turn with the ball far outside
A rapid roll into a steep turn that the pilot strongly feels
Rapid head movement during straight flight
An unnoticed gradual turn below about 2° per second
quiz.why: Rotation of about 2° per second or less is below the inner ear's detection threshold; leveling after such a turn feels like a bank the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies with a stick in the right hand. Right turns tend to dive and left turns tend to climb. What is the most likely cause?
options: Adverse yaw that grows larger in right turns at low speed
P-factor pulling the nose down in right turns
Cross-coupling as the arm pivots at the elbow
A trim tab set for a left-turning tendency
final_quiz.why: With a right-hand stick, diving in right turns and climbing in left turns is common because the arm rotates from the elbow; practice and holding the nose-on-horizon picture fix it [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

final_quiz.q: As a learner rolls right, the bank starts but the nose first swings left before following. What do you tell them?
options: Your rudder was too late; bring it in together with the aileron
You need more power before you start the roll
Your rudder was too early; wait until the bank is fully set
You need less back pressure as the bank goes in
final_quiz.why: If the bank starts before the nose turns, or the nose moves the opposite way, the rudder is late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Adverse yaw swings the nose away from the turn [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].

final_quiz.q: In a 15° left turn, your learner neutralizes the controls and the turn slowly stops. What is the fix?
options: Hold a little left aileron pressure, with rudder as needed
Add right aileron to keep the bank from steepening
Push the left rudder harder and leave the ailerons
Add power, since the turn stopped when the airspeed decayed
final_quiz.why: Shallow banks tend to level from lateral stability, so the pilot keeps a little aileron pressure into the bank, including rudder for yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: In a 30° right turn, the ball is right of center. Which correction fits?
options: Add left rudder and steepen the bank
Ease the right rudder, since the airplane is skidding
Add right rudder, or reduce the bank a little
Neutralize the rudder and add back pressure
final_quiz.why: Ball to the inside of the turn is a slip; step on the ball (right rudder), or decrease bank and/or increase the rate of turn [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

final_quiz.q: A learner keeps fixing altitude by staring at the altimeter and moving the yoke. What does the AFH say is wrong?
options: Nothing; the altimeter is the primary pitch reference for VFR turns
Using the yoke instead of trim to correct altitude in a turn
Not using the vertical speed indicator to lead the altimeter
Correcting while looking inside; fix pitch on the horizon first
final_quiz.why: Correcting pitch or bank while still looking inside is the most common beginner error [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]; correct pitch against the natural horizon and then cross-check the instruments [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: Turning left at 30° of bank from 180 to 090, where should the rollout begin?
final_quiz.why: Lead by half the bank, 15°. In a left turn the heading decreases toward 090, so begin at 090 + 15 = 105 [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner, as your learner, turns using mostly rudder with only a few degrees of bank, and the ball sits outside the turn. How do you name and fix it?
options: A slipping turn; add rudder in the direction of the turn
A skidding flat turn; bank the airplane and coordinate
An overbanking tendency; hold opposite aileron
A parallax error; change the sight picture
final_quiz.why: "Making skidding flat turns to avoid banking" is on the AFH list [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. The airplane turns by banking [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]], and a ball outside the turn shows a skid [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

final_quiz.q: On a hazy day near a VOR, which plan best manages collision risk in level turn practice?
options: You do all the scanning so the learner can concentrate on the turn
Use only the traffic display and fly the turns steeper
Climb above the haze layer and skip the clearing turns
Learner raises the wing, looks and calls it; you both keep watch
final_quiz.why: Raise the wing toward the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]; verbalize the clearing [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]; haze reduces detection and traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]; instructor and learner share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's level turns look good, but you suspect they are copying you without understanding. What fits the AIH advice?
options: Sign off the maneuver, since the performance meets the standards
Ask for a turn to a named heading at a new bank, then back
Fly three more demonstrations exactly as before
Give a written quiz on the four forces only
final_quiz.why: Have learners vary the maneuver slightly or combine it with other operations; those who do not understand the principles will probably not manage it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: In a 20° turn, the learner holds the nose steady on the horizon, but the bank slowly grows to 30° unnoticed. Which listed error is this?
options: Gaining proficiency in only one direction
Holding excessive rudder in the direction of turn
Leaning away from the direction of the turn
Holding the bank by watching only the nose
final_quiz.why: "Attempting to maintain a constant bank angle by referencing only the airplane's nose" is a listed error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]; use the cowling line and wingtips, then cross-check the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: A learner leans right during every left turn. Why does the AFH want it fixed right away?
options: It shifts the CG and changes the trim
It hides the ball from the learner's view
It sets up the Coriolis illusion every time the learner turns
It keeps the learner from properly learning the outside visual references
final_quiz.why: Leaning away from the turn to stay upright should be corrected immediately if the pilot is to learn the visual references [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

final_quiz.q: In a 30° level turn with constant power, airspeed slowly drops. What explains it?
options: The extra angle of attack adds induced drag
The horizontal lift component slows the airplane
Adverse yaw from the aileron held into the turn
The propeller loses thrust in a banked attitude
final_quiz.why: Holding altitude takes more angle of attack, which raises induced drag; airspeed drops in proportion to bank unless power is added [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner trimmed during a long 30° turn and, at wings level, the nose rises. What is the best coaching line?
options: "Start the rollout sooner next time"
"Add a little power as you roll the wings level"
"Hold a little forward pressure until you can retrim the airplane"
"Use more rudder toward the high wing"
final_quiz.why: If trim was used, forward elevator pressure may be needed until the trim is adjusted [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]; the AIH demonstration ends with reducing power and trimming at wings level [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

takeaways: The horizontal component of lift turns the airplane; the rudder only cancels adverse yaw.
Shallow banks tend to level, medium banks hold, steep banks roll in: hold, neutralize, or oppose.
Back pressure stays in through the whole turn; add power as the bank gets steeper.
Rudder timing shows on the nose: moves first means rudder early; bank first or nose away means rudder late.
Set bank by the cowling line and wingtips, then cross-check; correct posture and parallax early.
Lead the rollout by about half the bank, with aileron and rudder toward the high wing and back pressure coming out.
Clear before every turn, raising or lowering the wing toward the turn, and keep about 90 percent of attention outside.
cfi_notes: The sources differ on what the rudder does once established. PHAK 5-23 says once in the turn the rudder should not be needed [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]], and PHAK 6-4 says to relax aileron and rudder at the desired bank [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. The AFH says a shallow bank needs aileron into the turn including rudder, and a steep bank needs opposite aileron and rudder [[24:77|AFH 3-16]], with a slight slip from the outer wing's drag in steep turns [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. They agree only for medium banks. Teach "keep the ball centered" and let the airplane show what it needs.

The AIH sample demo says to neutralize the ailerons at the desired bank [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. That is right for a medium bank but not for a shallow one, where the AFH says to hold a little aileron into the turn [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Demonstrate at about 30° if you use that script word for word.

The AFH turn sequence says to add "either enough power or pitching up" [[24:72|AFH 3-11]]. The PHAK says the angle of attack must increase to hold altitude in any level turn, and power keeps the airspeed [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. Teach back pressure as always required and power as the way to hold airspeed.
PHAK 5-23's "about 79 percent" vertical lift at 44° of bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] does not fit cos 44° = 0.72; see the AI.II.D note before quoting it.

The AFH half-bank lead is a rule of thumb, and the AIH adds that the real lead depends on the type of turn, the turn rate and the roll-out rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A learner who rolls out slowly needs more lead.

Cross-coupling with a right-hand stick (dives in right turns, climbs in left) is in the AFH [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. In a yoke trainer you will more often see pitch changes from looking at the instruments or from parallax [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

The AFH and AIM both put clearing before every turn [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. The AIM's wing raise or dip before turning is the version to teach in a high-wing or low-wing trainer, and it fits easily into your demonstration.

AI.VIII.A (Straight-and-Level) covers trim procedure and the straight-flight references in depth; AI.II.D covers load factor; AI.IX.A covers overbanking and applies the left-seat parallax geometry to the right seat (no source covers that seat). Point learners there instead of repeating them in the turn lesson.
gaps: The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task, and the AFH gives none for a level turn; the examiner's judgment and your own standard fill that gap.
Power settings, pitch attitudes and how much rudder each direction needs come from the POH/AFM and from flying the specific airplane; no source here lists them.
No source here says what bank angle to introduce first; the AFH only says beginners should use small inputs and slow roll rates [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].
The AFH says instrument covers may be used "for the first several hours" [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] but gives no rule for when to take them off.
No source here describes the level turn sight picture from the right seat; see AI.IX.A for the parallax application.

activities.title: Read the level turn picture
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the picture.

pins.label: Natural horizon: the main attitude reference
Lowered wing against the ground: the bank seen outside
Attitude indicator: cross-check the bank angle
Altimeter: is the pitch holding altitude?
Turn coordinator: rate and direction, with the ball
Heading indicator: how far to the rollout

activities.title: Slip, skid or coordinated?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the turn it describes.

items.t: Ball to the inside of the turn
Rate of turn too slow for the bank
Too little right rudder in a right turn
Ball to the outside of the turn
Rate of turn too great for the bank
Pilot feels pushed toward the outside

activities.title: Work the turn numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Right turn at 30° of bank from 360 to 090. At what heading should the rollout start?
items.why: Lead = 30 / 2 = 15°. Turning right, the heading increases toward 090, so start at 090 - 15 = 075 [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

items.q: Left turn at 20° of bank from 090 to 270. At what heading should the rollout start?
items.why: Lead = 20 / 2 = 10°. Turning left, the heading decreases toward 270, so start at 270 + 10 = 280 [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

items.q: What is the rate of turn at 20° of bank and 100 knots true airspeed? (1,091 x tan bank / TAS)
At that rate, how many seconds does a 90° heading change take?
At standard rate, how many seconds does a 180° heading change take?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. 180 / 3 = 60 seconds.

items.q: In a level 30° turn, total lift must be how many times the weight so the vertical part still equals weight?
items.why: Application: vertical lift = total lift x cos 30° = total lift x 0.866. Setting that equal to weight: 1 / 0.866 = 1.15. The sources say vertical lift must equal weight [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] and total lift must increase [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

activities.title: True or false: references and instruments
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Instrument references should wait until the learner can fly the turn well by outside references.
cards.why: False. Instrument references should begin the first time each maneuver is introduced [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

cards.s: A bank error obvious at the wingtips may be hard for a beginner to see on the attitude indicator.
The turn coordinator shows the bank angle.
cards.why: False. It shows only the rate and direction of turn [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

cards.s: A pitch change of several inches against the horizon may show as only a tiny move of the attitude indicator's reference bar.
cards.why: True. That is why pitch is set on the horizon and only confirmed on the instruments [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

cards.s: An instructor may cover the flight instruments early in training to break a fixation habit.
cards.why: True, for the first several hours [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

cards.s: In a banked turn the pilot is pressed down into the seat, a feel cue worth teaching.
cards.why: True. The increased G of a turn presses the pilot into the seat [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

activities.title: Talk the learner through a level turn
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Clear the area: raise or lower the wing toward the turn, look, and call it
Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder, adding back pressure (and a little power)
At the desired bank, set the aileron for the bank class and hold the back pressure
Hold the picture on the horizon, scan for traffic, cross-check the instruments
About half the bank before the heading, aileron and rudder toward the high wing
Relax back pressure as the bank comes out; controls neutral at wings level
Reduce the added power and trim for straight-and-level

activities.title: First level turns, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFI with a pre-solo learner in a high-wing trainer. Straight-and-level is solid; today is the first lesson on level turns. The practice area is a little hazy.

steps.s: On the ground the learner asks, "So I steer it with my feet, like a car?"
options: Explain that bank turns it; the rudder only coordinates
Yes; the rudder turns the airplane and the ailerons just tilt it relative to the horizon
Tell them to use the rudder alone for small heading changes and ailerons for big ones
Skip it for now; the answer will become clear in the air once they feel a turn
steps.why: An airplane must be banked to turn; the horizontal component of lift turns it and the rudder offsets adverse yaw [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[24:72|AFH 3-11]].

steps.s: In the practice area the learner starts rolling left right away.
options: Stop: raise the left wing, look, and call the clearing
Ask ATC whether any traffic is nearby first, then continue the roll if none is reported
Have them turn right instead, since that side looks clearer, and continue the roll without any traffic check
Let it go, since you already looked to the left and saw nothing in the turn
steps.why: High-wing: raise the wing in the direction of the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]; correct any entry without a traffic check at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

steps.s: In a 30° left turn the nose sinks below the picture and the altimeter shows 80 feet low.
options: Take the controls immediately and demonstrate the turn again so they can see the picture
Coach less bank and more rudder to stop the descent and bring the altimeter back
Coach more back pressure to restore the picture, then check altitude
Coach full power and hold the same pitch until the altimeter shows the assigned altitude
steps.why: Back pressure keeps the vertical lift; correct pitch on the horizon, then cross-check [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

steps.s: In the next right turn the ball sits well to the left of center.
options: Coach more right rudder
Coach opposite aileron
Coach less bank and more power
Coach easing off the right rudder
steps.why: Ball outside the turn is a skid from too much right rudder; step on the ball [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

steps.s: Rolling out to a heading of 090 from a 30° turn, the learner overshoots by 15° every time.
options: Start the rollout exactly at 090 but roll out faster with more aileron
Start the rollout about 15° before 090 with coordinated controls
Use rudder alone to stop the turn on 090 while holding the bank angle with aileron
Use a shallower bank every time so that no lead is needed before the rollout
steps.why: Lead by about half the bank [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]; the lead also depends on the roll-out rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
